source.title: Erasing Conceptual Knowledge from Language Models
source.authors: Rohit Gandikota; Sheridan Feucht; Samuel Marks; David Bau

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates concept erasure and attacks on its own ELM models. It reports strong resistance to adversarial prompts but also a fine-tuning attack that brings some WMDP accuracy back, qualifying the robustness claim.
record.gate_note: Rows cover ELM's WMDP and Harry Potter evaluation, its reported GCG and BEAST attacks, linear probing, and the fine-tuning attack. The study does not test quantization, activation-direction ablation, prompt rephrasing, other languages, or in-context recovery. Comparisons with cited work outside the study's own experiments are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes ELM as a robust unlearning method (version F) and runs its own attacks on it. GCG and BEAST prompts fail to recover erased knowledge. Fine-tuning on the forget set partly recovers WMDP-Bio (29.7 to 42.2) and barely moves Cyber. It also measures near-chance erasure with retained MMLU (A), and gives baseline results for WHP, an original source, and RMU.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ELM gives near-random MCQ accuracy on erased concepts while keeping general capabilities and fluency, and that its resistance to adversarial attacks validates their approach. The fine-tuning recovery appears only in Appendix G.3. There they call it slight and below original levels, and say that retraining can bring knowledge back "but it is harder" without saying harder than what. It is not part of the main conclusion. The impact statement adds that undetected knowledge may remain.
record.recipe_differences: ELM uses self-classification-based distribution matching and low-rank updates; the study compares it with RMU, RepNoise, and WhoIsHarryPotter rather than reproducing their unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different erasure outcomes across models and benchmarks. ELM results also vary with inclusion of the fluency term for Qwen2.5-32B and Llama3-70B.

fits_no_version.finding: ELM disrupts activation norms in early layers on forget inputs, with a return to baseline by the middle layers. RMU's disruption persists across all layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ELM alters early-layer activation norms for erased-concept inputs while later-layer norms return to baseline.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated outcomes. Probe values are shown only in a figure and not given numerically. The adversarial prompt results include qualitative examples and the fine-tuning attack uses the original forget dataset rather than small or unrelated data.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Quantization, direction ablation, paraphrase, multilingual and in-context attacks on ELM.
Small, unrelated or loosely related relearning sets; a subset of forgotten facts; attack budget.
Activation-direction ablation, and non-linear or other analyses separating blocking from deletion.
Rephrasing, other languages (the authors note English only), and in-context information.
Robustness of ELM to quantization, direction ablation and the non-adversarial prompt attacks.

missing.what: RMU and RepNoise WMDP and MMLU results run by this study, e.g. Zephyr RMU 30.5/27.3 with MMLU 57.5 (WMDP authors' model); Llama3-8B RMU 49.4/37.0 with MMLU 40.1; Mistral RMU MMLU 27.1.
Probe results for RMU (near chance) and RepNoise (partial retention on Cyber).
GCG examples for RMU and RepNoise, which produce incoherent output before and after the attack.
Full fine-tuning variant of ELM: Bio 25.4, Cyber 27.1, but MMLU drops to 45.2.
MT-Bench general-ability values for ELM, e.g. Llama3-8B falls from 5.6 to 4.8.
Accuracy on closely related safe MMLU subjects falls slightly for both ELM and RMU after WMDP erasure (figure-only); the Limitations section also notes degradation on adjacent concepts.

record.verdict_notes: Repair of the quarantined Opus verdict. (1) The merge refused it because r30 had two row_fixes items. I merged them into one item with versions E, A and F and state absent. The state follows what the row measures, recovery by GCG, which matches the record and how r28 and r29 are handled. The problem text explains that the failed attack is the resistance A and F predict. (2) The earlier r31 fix linked only E, yet the A-supports and F-supports labels cite r31. I relinked it to E, A and F with state absent, so every label rests on rows linked to its version. (3) B label: Bio recovery is 12.5/34.7, about 36% of the gap, not 37%. (4) authors_conclusion: the earlier text said recovery was 'harder than for other models'. The paper only says 'harder' and names no comparison, so I fixed the wording. (5) A challenges reason: added the authors' explicit statements that WHP and RMU fail to erase, which justifies 'challenges' even though r25 and r26 are partial. (6) Added one missing item for the related-MMLU specificity drop (Figure 2, Section 5.4, and Limitations). Everything else is kept from the earlier verdict and checked against the text. Table 4 confirms that Mistral ELM is 28.7/26.4 and RepNoise is 35.3/39.6. Other checks: the G.3 fine-tuning numbers, G.1 (more than 5000 iterations versus 200 for the original models), the Table 3 HP-MCQ values, and the 4-choice HP-MCQ (Section 5.1). Earlier notes still hold. The record's r3 and r4 took RepNoise's Mistral numbers. The study proposes the method it attacks, so its robustness tests are limited and qualitative: GCG with one target prompt, a single BEAST example, and a fine-tuning attack with no stated budget. WHP is an original source; the A verdict on it comes from this study's own re-evaluation of the released model. The study itself is not an original, so the A labels are allowed. No instructions were found in the study text.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests ELM, not every current unlearning method, and does not establish that all simple attack types fail.
The attack fine-tunes on the original forget dataset; it does not test a small subset, unrelated examples, or loosely related examples.
No activation-direction ablation or direct test distinguishing deleted knowledge from knowledge blocked from access.
Tests GCG and BEAST adversarial prompts only; no paraphrase, other-language, or in-context-information recovery test.
Tests ELM against GCG, BEAST, and fine-tuning, but not quantization, direction ablation, or the other prompt conditions.
